blocks.text: Python, Java and C++ each ship a fast queue — you'll almost never write one from scratch in an interview. JavaScript is the exception. Here's what to use in each language, what the methods are called, and the traps that cost people marks.
The built-in queue in each language
The same small job in all four: put some numbers in a queue, then take them all out. They come out in the order they went in.

blocks.code:
from collections import deque

def serve_in_order(nums):
    q = deque()
    for x in nums:
        q.append(x)                 # enqueue at the back
    served = []
    while q:                        # while not empty
        served.append(q[0])         # look at the front
        q.popleft()                 # dequeue it: O(1)
    return served                   # the same order the items arrived in

blocks.text: The names differ, the ideas don't:

blocks.code:
enqueue     dequeue         front     empty?              size
JavaScript     q.push(x)   head++          q[head]   head === q.length   q.length - head
Python deque   append(x)   popleft()       q[0]      not q               len(q)
Java Queue     offer(x)    poll()          peek()    isEmpty()           size()
C++ queue      push(x)     pop() (void!)   front()   empty()             size()

items: **JavaScript: `shift()` in a loop.** `shift()` moves every remaining item one place, so it's O(n) — and n dequeues cost O(n²). With 100,000 items that's about 5 billion moves. Keep a head index (above), or a linked list.
**Python: `list.pop(0)`.** Same problem: O(n) per call. Use `collections.deque` and `popleft()`. (`queue.Queue` exists too, but it's for passing work between threads — it adds locks and is slower.)

**Java: mixing the two method families.** `offer / poll / peek` return `false` or `null` when they can't do their job; `add / remove / element` **throw an exception** instead. And `int x = q.poll();` on an empty queue crashes with a `NullPointerException`, because `null` can't become an `int`. Check `isEmpty()` first.
**Java: `ArrayDeque` vs `LinkedList`.** Both implement `Queue`; `ArrayDeque` is faster and uses less memory. It doesn't allow `null` items, which is rarely a problem.

**C++: `pop()` returns nothing.** Read `front()` first, then `pop()`. Calling `front()` or `pop()` on an empty queue is **undefined behaviour** — no error, just wrong results or a crash. Check `empty()` first.

blocks.text: **n** players stand in a circle, numbered 1 to n, and pass a potato around. Each round, the potato is passed **k − 1** times, and whoever then holds it — the **k-th** holder — leaves the game. In what order do the players leave? (This is the **Josephus problem**.)
A circle is a queue that never ends: the **front** player holds the potato, and passing it on means **dequeue the front, enqueue them at the back**. Leaving means dequeue without enqueueing again.

blocks.alt: Hot potato with players 1 to 5 and k = 2. Start: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. 1 passes and goes to the back: 2, 3, 4, 5, 1. 2 is holding the potato, so 2 leaves: 3, 4, 5, 1. 3 passes: 4, 5, 1, 3. 4 leaves: 5, 1, 3. The full leaving order is 2, 4, 1, 5, 3.

elements.text: ... and so on: the full order is 2, 4, 1, 5, 3
elements.originalText: ... and so on: the full order is 2, 4, 1, 5, 3

blocks.text: Each pass is one dequeue and one enqueue, both O(1), and there are about k passes per player: **O(n · k)** time, **O(n)** space. Python's `deque.rotate(-(k - 1))` does all the passing in one call. Remember this **rotate** move — it comes back when we build a stack out of a single queue.

blocks.caption: Each round passes the potato k − 1 times, then the holder leaves.

items: Python: `collections.deque` with `append` / `popleft`. Java: `Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>()` with `offer` / `poll` / `peek`. C++: `std::queue` with `push` / `front` / `pop`.
JavaScript has no queue: use an array plus a head index, never `shift()` in a loop.
Check for empty **before** dequeueing — each language fails differently, some silently.
Dequeue-then-enqueue **rotates** a queue: the trick behind round robin and hot potato.
